newsitem.title: USA: Miami eyes bankruptcy court for liquidation model.
newsitem.headline: Miami eyes bankruptcy court for liquidation model.

text.p: Miami will turn to the corporate bankruptcy liquidation statutes for guidance in drafting its contingency plan on how to dissolve the city, City Manager Ed Marquez said Wednesday.
The plan would only be implemented if voters decide in a Sept 4 referendum that Miami should be dissolved and its government absorbed into the Metro-Dade County government.

The city commission must approve a plan spelling out what would become of the city's assets and liabilities by Aug. 4. But Marquez said there is no model to base that on because no other city has ever dissolved itself.
"I don't know of any. We have ghost towns, but that doesn't help any," Marquez said.

Other cities have merged their governments, as Jacksonville did when it joined Florida's Duval County government structure. But that is not a good model because it did not involve the liquidation of city assets, Marquez said.

"We'll probably model it after bankruptcy law," with the city commission acting as the equivalent of a corporate board, Marquez told the state-appointed oversight board that is guiding Miami's recovery from a $68 million deficit.

The city's assets include considerable land holdings and several buildings. Its liabilities include about $370 million of general obligation and special obligation bonds, with all but about $12 million of that insured.
Marquez said the dissolution referendum had already raised concern among bond rating agencies and the companies that insure Miami's bonds.
"They were more concerned about our dissolution plan than our (fiscal) recovery plan," said Marquez, who met in New York with the rating agencies and bond insurers last week.

Disgruntled citizens collected enough petition signatures to put the dissolution referendum on the ballot after three top city officials were indicted on charges of conspiring to solicit kickbacks on city contracts.

After they resigned last fall, an interim city manager discovered the $68 million deficit in the $275 million budget for fiscal 1997. Gov. Lawton Chiles appointed a financial oversight board to guide the city's recovery.
The board signed off last month on a five-year recovery plan that balances Miami's budget with union concessions, cuts in services, new fees and improved collections.
Still unresolved is whether the oversight board must approve the city's dissolution plan.
"It does seem to me the oversight board would have a role in that," Bobby Brochin, the board's attorney said.
The board's intergovernmental agreement with the city requires board approval for all financial transactions, he said.
But Marquez said the dissolution plan would involve mainly matters of policy, which should be left to the city commission.
"There are policy calls as to which assets you keep in trust for the benefit of the people and which you don't," Marquez said.
The board asked Brochin to research the issue. The dissolution plan would require liquidation of the city and all its assets by the end of 1998.
